module.subdomains_passive.checks: Complements certificate transparency logs with other free public sources: HackerTarget, RapidDNS, Anubis, AlienVault OTX, urlscan.io, Wayback Machine and, with an optional key, SecurityTrails. Checks which of the first names still resolve.
module.subdomains_passive.fix:
Export the scan's list of subdomains and compare it with your inventory (DNS host console, application list, internal map): every name must have a known owner and purpose.
For an unknown or forgotten name: first check that it really belongs to your domain, then delete its DNS record (A, AAAA or CNAME) from the zone and shut down the server or service behind it.
Names that no longer resolve come from archives: there is nothing to delete in the DNS, but check that no CNAME remains pointing to a terminated third-party service (subdomain takeover modules).
For each name that resolves but must not be public (staging, administration, internal tools): restrict access (VPN, allow-list of addresses, strong authentication) or remove it from the public DNS and serve it through an internal DNS.
Avoid putting a sensitive hint in a name (customer, project, software version): names end up in public certificates, web archives and scanning engines.
Run this scan again after every major release and at least once a quarter, to spot early a name that appeared without your decision.
module.subdomains_passive.fix_snippet:
# Bash
while read -r name; do
  echo "$name $(dig +short "$name" | tr '\n' ' ')"
done < subdomains.txt

# PowerShell
Get-Content subdomains.txt | ForEach-Object { Resolve-DnsName $_ -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Name, Type, IPAddress, NameHost }
module.subdomains_passive.title: Subdomains (complementary passive sources)
module.subdomains_passive.why: No single source sees everything: a forgotten subdomain sometimes appears only in a web archive or a scanning engine. The more complete the map, the less unknown attack surface remains.
